reference_title: Drilled Shafts: Construction Procedures and LRFD Design Methods

sections.title: Responsibilities
sections.body: [pp. 15-1 to 15-3] Chapter introduction (p. 15-1): unlike driven piles, whose driving resistance indicates nominal resistance, successful drilled shaft installation can only be assessed by verifying conformance with the contract documents and the approved Drilled Shaft Installation Plan and consistency with the procedures of the successful technique and test shafts; inspection also identifies unanticipated conditions that might jeopardize performance or integrity. Complete written records communicate the work and, with integrity testing (Chapter 16), are the primary means of identifying and initially assessing problems; they are the basis for evaluating 'differing site condition' (DSC) claims (FHWA GT-15, 1996; Section 2.6). References: NHI Course No. 132070 'Drilled Shaft Foundation Inspection' (2002); ADSC/DFI 'Drilled Shaft Inspector's Manual' (2nd Edition, 2004); ADSC videos. Responsibilities: on design-bid-build the inspector works for the owner or its construction management firm; on design-build more typically for the design-builder's independent quality control organization, communicating with the designer-of-record, the design-builder's staff and the owner's QA staff. The inspector monitors construction to make records and gives timely information on unanticipated conditions and deviations, communicating with the contractor but not directing the work; only the contractor directs operations. Inspectors must be qualified by training and experience: complete a course such as NHI 132070 and be certified, and have prior experience or work under an experienced inspector; typically a trained technician, or a geotechnical engineer experienced with drilled shafts. Attend pre-construction meetings and get a briefing from the foundation designer or geotechnical engineer. Duties: attend meetings and safety training; know site conditions, subsurface conditions, contract documents and payment provisions, the current approved Installation Plan (Section 14.9), and installation criteria and tolerances; have calibrated equipment (15.2.1) and blank forms (15.4); coordinate with surveying; observe and document all activities (15.2), slurry tests (15.2.3) and concrete tests and cylinder sampling (15.2.6); immediately inform the foundation design engineer, resident engineer and/or owner of unanticipated conditions, problems or non-conforming work; share concerns and data with the contractor; measure and record pay quantities. Keep the relevant documents in the field (plans, specifications, latest Plan, engineer's instructions, nearest boring logs) and set up communication procedures beforehand; the designer and/or geotechnical engineer must assess the inspector's information and respond quickly, since delays can jeopardize excavation stability and performance. The inspector must also judge observed activities and raise issues promptly, and may share observations with the superintendent so the contractor can act, while still documenting and reporting them. The contractor determines conforming means and methods, installs per the approved Plan consistent with technique and load test shafts, and is responsible for structural integrity.
key_points: Inspection verifies conformance with contract documents, the Installation Plan and technique/test shaft procedures
Records plus integrity testing are the primary basis for assessing problems and DSC claims
Inspector monitors, records and reports; does not direct the contractor
Inspectors trained (e.g., NHI 132070), certified and experienced or supervised
Immediately report unanticipated conditions or non-conforming work; engineers respond quickly
Contractor responsible for means and methods and structural integrity
sections.applicability: Field inspection on all drilled shaft projects; inspector qualification requirements

sections.title: Inspection Activities
sections.body: [pp. 15-4 to 15-6] The inspector observes all stages from set-up to completion of concrete placement, including removal of temporary casing (15.2.1 to 15.2.7). Table 15-1 is a sample checklist; a comprehensive project-specific checklist should be developed. Table 15-1 groups: contractor and equipment arrival (Installation Plan submitted and approved; approved mix design, trial mix and slump loss test, extended test if placement over two hours; Slurry Management Plan; pre-construction conference; base sampling or coring readiness; protection of structures; site preparation; tools, casing size, slurry mixing equipment, manufacturer's representative, de-sander, tremie, forms); technique shaft (location, installation, cutoff below grade, approval of revised procedures); excavation and cleaning (location and tolerances, benchmark, core holes and Rock Core form, slurry tests and level, excavation forms, casing, vertical alignment, depth, excavation time limit, over-reaming, bottom condition); reinforcing cage (sizes and configuration, tying, spacers, splices, secured against settling and floating, top elevation); concrete placement (slurry tested, tremie height above base, flap valve or 'pig', tremie embedment, free-fall in dry shafts only, placement time limit, placement and volume forms, overflow until good concrete, casing removal, acceptance tests); post installation (casing removed to elevation, integrity testing, tolerances, forms complete, pay items).
key_points: Observe all stages from set-up to concrete completion and casing removal
Develop a project-specific checklist like Table 15-1
tables: Table 15-1: Sample Drilled Shaft Inspector's Checklist - 58 yes/no/N/A items grouped as contractor and equipment arrive on site, technique shaft, shaft excavation and cleaning, reinforcing cage, concrete placement, and post installation
sections.applicability: All drilled shaft construction inspection; QA activities during construction

sections.title: Set-Up
sections.body: [p. 15-4] Before installation: attend pre-construction meetings; collect the project documents for the shaft; know the drawings, specifications and approved Installation Plan; observe site conditions; check and calibrate inspection equipment (measuring tape, weighted sounding tape, 4-ft level, carpenter's square, slurry testing equipment, concrete testing equipment, sample molds); collect forms and review entries with the geotechnical engineer; verify tools match the Plan's equipment list and drilling tool dimensions match the design diameter and any rock socket; check casing (15.2.2) and the rebar cage (15.2.5); verify communication protocol and contact numbers; photograph tools, casing, cage and equipment; use safety equipment and attend safety training.
key_points: Know documents and Plan; calibrate equipment (tape, weighted tape, 4-ft level, square, slurry and concrete kits)
Check tools against the Plan and design diameter; check casing and cage
Set up communications; photograph equipment; safety
sections.applicability: Inspector set-up tasks before drilled shaft installation

sections.title: Casing
sections.body: [p. 15-7] Verify temporary casing diameter, wall thickness, length and tip reinforcement or bands against the Plan; for permanent casing verify dimensions and steel grade against the plans, straightness and cross-section distortion within tolerance, and documented splice inspection and weld testing. Check casing location (offsets from survey points) and verticality (4-ft level or plumb bob) as set; note the advancing method and any unexpected resistance, deformation, tilting or 'walking'; record start and completion times and delays including splicing; record top and bottom elevations (permanent casing within tolerance of the drawings); for temporary casing record extraction times and method.
key_points: Verify casing dimensions, grade, straightness, splices
Check location and verticality; record installation difficulties, times and elevations
Record temporary casing extraction times and method
sections.applicability: Inspecting temporary and permanent casing installation

sections.title: Drilling Fluid
sections.body: [p. 15-7] The drilling fluid should follow the approved Plan, slurry mixed, placed and treated per the manufacturer and the Plan. Observe slurry tests for type and frequency per the specifications (procedures in FHWA, 2002; summarized in Chapter 5); tests are usually by the contractor and monitored by the inspector, who records all results and confirms compliance with the specified criteria or, if not specified, the manufacturer's recommendations. If slurry is inadequate or properties cannot be achieved, the contractor must modify the mix; share any inspector test results. Proper slurry performance is essential to wet construction, so the inspector must understand slurry use and testing (Chapter 5).
key_points: Fluid per the approved Plan and manufacturer
Record all slurry test results against specified criteria (Chapter 5)
Contractor modifies the mix if performance or properties are inadequate
sections.applicability: Inspecting drilling fluid use and testing

sections.title: Drilled Shaft Excavation
sections.body: [pp. 15-8 to 15-11] During excavation: verify top location within tolerance; document equipment and tool changes with depths against the Plan; verify procedures; check verticality with a 4-ft level on the Kelly bar; sound depth often and log elevation and time, with temporary casing bottom elevation at the same times; dry method: casing sealed in an impermeable stratum, infiltration rate and base water depth within limits; wet method: slurry or water level at or above the specified minimum at all times; perform or observe slurry testing; describe cuttings, correlate with borings and previous shafts, note elevations of material changes; document obstructions (times, equipment); record top of rock, its condition and any sloping surface; verify and log a required probe hole (preferably before excavation, at the contractor's option). Cross-section is usually estimated from tool and casing diameters and concrete volume, which is very imprecise; a borehole caliper, mechanical or sonic (Figure 15-1), is recommended for test shafts or suspected voids. Document final bottom cleaning: equipment, check method, results and times. Bottom cleanliness: (a) weighted tape soundings at four sides and the center to confirm a firm base without soft, mushy material (a small foot for soil, Figure 15-2; on rock a short bar such as a #18 for a sound 'thump'); (b) uncommonly a neutral buoyancy rod; (c) a video device such as the Shaft Inspection Device (SID, Figure 15-3), a gas-pressurized diving bell set at the center and four orthogonal sides with camera and sediment depth gauges, often used for non-redundant and end-bearing shafts. Document unusual conditions (boulders or obstructions, caving, bottom heave, soil or rock differing from borings, slow drilling, fluid loss, ground loss, excavation time exceeding the limit, anything affecting friction or end bearing) and immediately notify the engineers. Inspect from the surface; personnel should not enter a shaft unless absolutely necessary and only with all safety precautions. The engineer should review each excavation log for conformance and compatibility with the resistance requirements.
key_points: Log tools, depths, times, verticality, casing elevations, cuttings and top of rock
Dry method: casing seal and infiltration limits; wet method: fluid level at or above minimum
Caliper recommended for test shafts or suspected voids (Figure 15-1)
Base: weighted tape at center and four sides; SID camera for non-redundant or end-bearing shafts
Report unusual conditions immediately; do not enter shafts unless absolutely necessary

sections.title: Placement of Reinforcement
sections.body: [pp. 15-11 to 15-12] Reinforcement arrives as bars for site fabrication or as pre-assembled cages. Tasks: verify coupon samples if required; bars and cages supported off the ground and protected from contamination; cage grade, dimensions, arrangement, sizes and spacing per drawings and specifications; intersections tied as required; centering devices and bottom spacers ('boots') per the Plan; CSL tubes of specified material, undamaged and straight, full length, watertight couplers and caps, securely attached in the required arrangement; other embedded items (base grouting systems, TIP cables, bi-directional devices, instrumentation), usually checked by a specialty subconsultant; observe lifting for damage or distortion; splices made while lowering per the drawings (lap lengths, mechanical splices, staggering); temporary stiffeners removed and missing centering devices replaced while lowering. Be alert to procedures that dislodge soil or rock (rapid lowering, eccentric cage, missing centralizers, protrusions); sound the base after placing the cage and inform the engineer of a noticeable change, who may require removing the cage and re-cleaning.
key_points: Check cage per drawings, ties, centralizers, boots, CSL tubes and embedded items
Watch lifting, splicing, stiffener removal
Sound the base after cage placement; engineer may require removal and re-cleaning

sections.title: Concrete Placement
sections.body: [pp. 15-12 to 15-15] Concrete placement must be carefully inspected and documented, also to assess anomalies found by integrity testing (Chapter 16); it covers sampling and testing (FHWA 2002; Section 7.7) and placement. Sampling and testing: delivery ticket per load (mix and volume); mix tested and approved at an ambient temperature equal to or greater than at placement, since slump loss depends strongly on temperature (especially deep, large wet shafts); batch time within range; slump or slump flow, temperature and air tests at the specified frequency, and occasional slump loss tests on the first load for long placements or hot weather; cylinders at the specified frequency, stored properly; watch for segregation, clumping, insufficient slump. Placement: if infiltration rate or base water exceed limits, fill with water or slurry and place by the wet method; tremie or pump line of minimum diameter, long enough, clean, watertight, marked at intervals not over 5 feet; CSL tubes filled with water and capped; bottom flap valve or a proper 'pig'; tremie within the maximum height above the base at the start and embedded the minimum depth throughout; in wet excavations internal fluid pressure above external hydrostatic pressure; temporary casing pulled slowly and vertically with concrete kept inside it; dry method: free-fall within the limit without hitting the cage or sides; keep a placement log (15.4) and a plot of actual and theoretical volume versus elevation for bulging, necking and instability; overpour until good concrete reaches the top, or above cutoff the minimum in the Plan if chipping; for wet shafts total placement time from first batch to end of placement and casing removal within the approved maximum from slump loss testing; report unusual observations. Record volume versus elevation (especially for load test shafts) using a weighted tape after each truck, minus volume in the tremie; excess volume indicates overbreak or voids (e.g., karstic cavities), and a sudden rise relative to volume may indicate a cave-in (Figure 15-4). Measure concrete level before and after removing each casing section and compare the drop with the steel volume removed to detect voids outside the casing. Pump stroke counters need calibration; bucket counts give approximate volume.
key_points: Mix approved at ambient temperature at least that of placement; check batch time, slump, temperature, cylinders
Tremie: minimum diameter, watertight, marked at 5-ft max intervals, flap valve or pig, minimum embedment throughout
Keep concrete inside temporary casing; pull casing slowly and vertically
Plot actual vs. theoretical volume vs. elevation (Figure 15-4); check level drop at each casing removal
Wet shafts: total placement time within the slump-loss-based maximum
sections.applicability: Inspecting concrete sampling, testing and placement in drilled shafts

sections.title: Completed Drilled Shaft
sections.body: [p. 15-15] At completion: obtain the surveyed as-built location and top of concrete elevation; complete a summary installation form of as-built dimensions and elevations (15.4); for unit pricing determine and agree pay quantities with the contractor; compile and file records; update project control summaries.
key_points: As-built location and top elevation; summary form; pay quantities agreed; file records
sections.applicability: Inspector tasks at completion of each drilled shaft

sections.title: Common Problems
sections.body: [pp. 15-15 to 15-16] The vast majority of shafts are built without loss of resistance or integrity defects; problems likely fall into the categories of Table 15-2, which the inspector should discuss with the engineers for the project conditions and method and watch for. Table 15-2 (after Baker et al., 1993; O'Neill, 1991) problems and causes: off location or out of plumb (set-up or alignment); insufficient embedment (bearing stratum misidentified or length mismeasured); crack (hit by equipment early in curing); bulge or neck (uncased soft zones); caving (improper casing or slurry, no weighting agent, casing not sealed); reduced side resistance from mudcake (slurry not agitated, concrete not timely); temporary casing stuck (ineffective extraction equipment, soil set-up, wedged casing); horizontal separation or severe necking (concrete adhering to pulled casing, inadequate casing penetration into concrete); horizontal sand lens (tremie pulled out, insufficient workability, insufficient head in casing); soil intrusion (telescoping casing spill, low slump, close bars); soft bottom or CSL anomaly near the bottom (incomplete cleaning, sloughing, sedimentation); voids outside cage (low slump, large aggregate, close bars); concrete defects (leaking tremie joints, tremie not at bottom or raised above concrete, flow into annulus between casings, inadequate slump for duration, sediment in slurry); honeycombing, washout or water channels (concrete into water, groundwater head, bleed water); folded-in debris (insufficient cleaning, sand in slurry); clogged tremie (insufficient slump or retention, dirty pipe, segregation); cage lifted (light cage, tremie too deep, cage caught, concrete arch); cage settles (missing spacers, insufficient support or stiffness).
key_points: Most shafts have no problems; know the Table 15-2 categories and their causes
Concrete placement and casing extraction errors cause most integrity defects (sand lenses, necking, voids)
Cage uplift from light cage, deep tremie embedment or arching; settlement from missing spacers

sections.title: Records and Forms
sections.body: [pp. 15-17 to 15-18] Agencies typically have standard forms (cage fabrication checklist, permanent casing checklist, excavation log, bottom inspection form, concrete placement forms), often attached to the specification; otherwise use the Appendix E sample forms (with completed examples). Procedures: each page identifies project, location, structure, shaft number, date and page, and the inspector(s) with times of change; record elevations rather than depths (depths only if the reference elevation is surveyed and documented); record date and time of start and completion of each activity and of interruptions, and for repetitive operations each tool insertion and removal with periodic excavation levels, using a 24-hour clock. Keep a daily report: weather and river level, equipment and work force, repairs, general activities, delays, time and materials for unanticipated tasks such as obstructions, information from the contractor or engineer, instructions to the crew by the superintendent, time on unrelated activities. File all records centrally per document control and distribute logs promptly to the resident engineer and foundation design engineer.
key_points: Agency forms or Appendix E sample forms
Record elevations, not depths; 24-hour clock; start, end and interruptions of every activity
Daily report for weather, equipment, delays, obstructions, instructions
Central filing; prompt distribution to the engineers
sections.applicability: Documentation requirements for all drilled shaft projects

sections.title: Summary
sections.body: [p. 15-18] The chapter covered the inspector's responsibilities and tasks, with checklists and forms. The inspector is not just an observer and recorder but must proactively identify issues and communicate them promptly to the resident, foundation design and geotechnical engineers; the inspector has no authority to direct the contractor but should share observations with the superintendent so the contractor can act while still possible. Inspection records are the only reliable information verifying installation per the contract documents and approved Plan, the principal means of evaluating completed shafts, and the basis for evaluating DSC claims and compensating additional work.
key_points: Inspector proactive in identifying and reporting issues; never directs the contractor
Records verify conformance, evaluate completed shafts and support DSC claim evaluation
sections.applicability: Overview of Chapter 15, Inspection and Records.
